channel.title: Higher Ed News Digest
channel.description: A daily spoken brief on higher education policy, online learning, edtech, enrolment and accreditation. Read by Serena.

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Thursday, 12 November 2026
item.description:
Coverage window: Tuesday, November 10 through Thursday, November 12, 2026. 16 stories plus the Competitor Spotlight.

In this episode

  1. NAFSA Snapshot: Six in Ten Colleges Lost International Graduate Students This Fall, by an Average of 13 Percent
  2. Penn State Faces a $124 Million Budget Gap, Most of It From Lower Tuition Revenue, and Plans No Layoffs
  3. Accreditor Scrutiny of Maine's YourPace Online Program: Rapid Growth, Heavy Transfer Credit and a Suspended Approval
  4. Colleges Tell DHS the $70,000 OPT Fee Would Cost Them Tens of Millions a Year; Still No CPT Ruling
  5. Student Success Leaders Survey: 32 Percent See No Measurable Student Gains From AI, and 27 Percent Are Unsure
  6. American Public Education Raises Guidance, but Says Non-Health Online Programs Are Where the Weakness Is
  7. Coursera Adopts a Poison Pill After an Unnamed Investor Builds a 14.7 Percent Stake
  8. Blackboard Co-Founder Matthew Pittinsky Returns as CEO, Promising an AI-Driven LMS
  9. Three-Year Degrees Keep Spreading, but Early Adopters Struggle to Fill Them
  10. Strada's State Opportunity Index: Positive Return on a Public Degree Stays at 70 Percent; Paid Work-Based Learning Stuck at 43
  11. WashU Says It Can View Students' Claude Chat Logs in Misconduct Cases
  12. Harvard's Education School Releases an "AI Guidance by Age" Matrix for Course and Assessment Design
  13. Price Sensitivity Reaches Wealthier Privates: Baylor Projects a $30 Million Deficit, Boston University Misses Revenue by $42 Million
  14. Alvernia University Plans to Absorb Marian University Across State Lines
  15. Craig Trainor, Author of ED's Anti-DEI Guidance, Will Lead the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division
  16. Senate Passes the RISE Act, Letting Students Use K-12 Records to Document Disabilities
  17. Competitor Spotlight: SNHU, plus University of Phoenix (not tracked); ASU Online, Purdue Global and UMGC

One thing to watch: Maine's YourPace review shows what an accreditor asks of a fast-growing online program: faculty ratios, transfer-credit sources, time to completion and identity verification.

Sources

International students

  • Colleges report declines in international enrollment amid federal restrictions — Higher Ed Dive
  • International Student Interest in U.S. Surges After Midterms — Inside Higher Ed
  • Interest in US surges as study destination up 40% after midterms — The PIE News
  • Colleges Say OPT Fee Would Cost Tens of Millions — Inside Higher Ed
  • Immigration Lawsuit Challenges DHS for Restricting Student Internships — Forbes

Institutional finance

  • Penn State Wrestles With $124M Budget Hole — Higher Ed Dive
  • Here's the Latest News on Campus Finance — The Chronicle of Higher Education
  • Baylor Stares Down $30M Deficit — Higher Ed Dive
  • Boston University misses revenue projections by $42M — Higher Ed Dive
  • Alvernia University Plans to Acquire Marian U in Wisconsin — Inside Higher Ed
  • Alvernia University to acquire Marian University — Higher Ed Dive

Online programs and accreditation

  • Amid Accreditor Scrutiny, Maine Officials Defend 'YourPace' Program — Inside Higher Ed
  • UMPI YourPace program changes — Bangor Daily News
  • As 3-Year Degrees Proliferate, Some Pioneers Face Roadblocks — Inside Higher Ed

AI and student success

  • The Priority? Student Success. The Challenge? Capacity. — Inside Higher Ed
  • Survey: Student Success Leaders Weigh Ahead to 2027 — Inside Higher Ed
  • WashU can see students' AI chat logs in misconduct cases. What do students think? — Student Life
  • New AI Learning Matrix Brings Nuance to 'Wild West' Moment — Inside Higher Ed

Business of online education

  • American Public Education Reports Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results — American Public Education
  • Am. Public Education (APEI) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript — The Motley Fool
  • Coursera 8-K Exhibit 99.1 — SEC
  • Coursera adopts poison pill after investor reaches 14.7% stake — Investing.com

Edtech and platforms

  • Blackboard Co-Founder Matthew Pittinsky Returns as CEO — PR Newswire
  • Matthew Pittinsky Returns to the Helm at Blackboard — Campus Technology
  • Blackboard Goes Back to the Future (Sort Of) — On EdTech

Public perception and outcomes

  • States Make Progress on Outcomes-Based Higher Education — Inside Higher Ed
  • 2026 State Opportunity Index by Strada Education Foundation — GlobeNewswire

Policy and legal

  • Anti-DEI Trump Official to Lead DOJ Civil Rights Office — Inside Higher Ed
  • DOJ Hires Ex-Jim Jordan Staffer as Civil Rights Chief — Washington Examiner
  • Bill Supporting College Students With Disabilities Advances — Inside Higher Ed

Competitor Spotlight

  • SNHU Marks Record Fall Commencement — SNHU
  • SNHU Celebrates Largest Fall Commencement (2025) — SNHU
  • University of Phoenix expands online degree with new three-year bachelor's in Information Technology — PR Newswire

Higher Ed News Digest is published every Monday and Thursday.

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Monday, 9 November 2026
item.description:
Coverage window: Saturday, November 7 through Monday, November 9, 2026, plus late-week items not previously covered. 15 stories plus the Competitor Spotlight.

In this episode

  1. Justice Department Sues Penn State Over In-State Tuition for Undocumented Students
  2. University of Phoenix Forecasts Lower Revenue for Fiscal 2027 and Blames AI Search
  3. Cornell's Faculty Senate Votes No Confidence in the Administration, 75 to 50
  4. After the Midterms, Experts Say Closing a $17 Billion Pell Shortfall Comes Before a Bigger Pell Grant
  5. Young Voters Went 66 to 31 Democratic, and College Students Voted Almost Exactly Like Non-Students
  6. UChicago Will Require an AI-Free First-Year Writing Course, as Eastern Illinois Students Ask for Rules on Faculty AI Use
  7. Top-Down AI Rollouts Meet Organized Faculty Resistance: San José State's Targets, a Cal State Labor Charge and a Faculty Poll
  8. Big Ten Peers Add Online Credentials: Illinois Law's Master's for Non-Lawyers and Purdue's Cybersecurity and Applied AI Programs
  9. Laureate's Revenue Rises 21 Percent While Stride's Adult Learning Revenue Falls 34 Percent
  10. Comments on the $70,000 OPT Fee Close Today; No Ruling Yet After the CPT Injunction Hearing
  11. UW–Madison Names Three Chancellor Finalists, Including UConn's President, and Not the Interim
  12. North Dakota State Warns of Faculty Cuts After a 3 Percent Enrollment Drop Driven by Retention
  13. Income-Driven Repayment Discharges Become Taxable Again, With Some Borrowers Facing Up to $12,000 in Added Tax
  14. College of Southern Nevada Builds No-Cost, AI-Assisted Mastery Courseware for a Course Required in 50 Programs
  15. Ohio State Keeps Leslie Wexner's Name on Its Buildings Without a Full Review
  16. Competitor Spotlight: UMGC; ASU Online, Purdue Global and SNHU

One thing to watch: Phoenix is the third online operator to blame AI search for lost inquiries and the first to cut its revenue forecast over it; its growth came from employer channels that search cannot intercept.

Sources

Courts and civil rights

  • DOJ sues Penn State over in-state tuition for undocumented students — Higher Ed Dive
  • DOJ Sues Penn State Over In-State Tuition for Noncitizens — Inside Higher Ed
  • Trump administration sues Penn State over tuition for immigrant students — Spotlight PA

The business of online education

  • Phoenix Education Partners, Inc. Reports Fourth Quarter and Fiscal Year 2026 Results — Business Wire
  • PXED Q4 FY2026 Earnings Call: AI Search Weighs on FY2027 Outlook — TradingKey
  • Laureate Education Reports Financial Results for the Third Quarter and Nine Months Ended September 30, 2026 — GlobeNewswire
  • Stride reports first quarter 2027 financial results — GlobeNewswire

Leadership and governance

  • Cornell Faculty Vote No Confidence in Administration — Inside Higher Ed
  • Cornell faculty vote no confidence in president over handling of rape case — Philadelphia Inquirer (AP)
  • UW-Madison chancellor finalists announced — Spectrum News
  • University of Wisconsin says UConn president is finalist for chancellor role — WFSB
  • Ohio State Keeps Wexner's Name on Buildings — Inside Higher Ed

Policy and politics

  • How Can Democrats Make the Most of Their Win? — Inside Higher Ed
  • The Incoming Lawmakers Who Worked in Higher Ed — Inside Higher Ed
  • ED Issues Workforce Pell FAQs; Courts Continue Changing Professional Degree List — UPCEA
  • Students with discharged IDR loans now face huge tax bills — Higher Ed Dive

Perceptions and the midterms

  • 2026 Youth Vote — CIRCLE, Tufts University
  • Young people turned out in near-record numbers — Fortune (via The Conversation)
  • The Exit Polls from A–Z: What Motivated Voters in 2026 — American Enterprise Institute
  • Democrats Narrowed the Diploma Divide. But It's Still Wide. — The Chronicle of Higher Education

AI in teaching and learning

  • New in AI: UChicago Rethinks Writing, EIU Students Want Faculty Rules — Inside Higher Ed
  • How to navigate AI adoption, with faculty and student input — Higher Ed Dive

Online programs and edtech

  • College of Law announces online master's program, certificates for non-legal professionals — The Daily Illini
  • Purdue launches Online Cybersecurity Programs to address emerging digital threats — WBIW
  • Purdue's online cybersecurity degree, AI graduate certificate prepare professionals for emerging digital threats — Purdue University
  • Instructional design first: AI-assisted courseware for mastery and learner agency — eCampus News

International students

  • NAFSA Comment Letter: DHS Proposed OPT Fee Rule — NAFSA
  • The Trump Administration's Proposed STEM OPT Fee — American Immigration Council
  • CPT lawsuit: DHS defense — Immigration Analytics

Finance

  • Here's the Latest News on Campus Finance — The Chronicle of Higher Education

Competitor Spotlight

  • UMGC and Newstate University Announce New Transfer Credit Agreement — UMGC

Higher Ed News Digest is published every Monday and Thursday.

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Saturday, 7 November 2026
item.description:
Coverage window: Friday, November 6 through Saturday, November 7, 2026. 15 stories plus the Competitor Spotlight.

In this episode

  1. Harmeet Dhillon, Architect of the Justice Department's Campaign Against Colleges, Resigns From the Civil Rights Division
  2. Repeal Is Off the Table: Democrats' Realistic Options on Loan Caps Narrow to Reclassifying Nursing and Allied Health as Professional Degrees
  3. Strategic Education Takes a $134 Million Write-Down on Its Australian Arm as Capella and Strayer Enrollment Slips 1.1 Percent
  4. Covista, the Former Adtalem, Posts a 13th Straight Quarter of Growth With Walden Enrollment Up 12.8 Percent
  5. Perdoceo Discloses Terms for South University: $130 Million to $150 Million at Closing, and a Warning That AI Search Is Cutting Inquiries
  6. Chegg's Revenue Falls 40 Percent as the CEO Says AI "Hit Our Business Hard"; the Pivot Is Internships, Skilling and Three College Pilots
  7. WCET Reads the Final Accreditation Rule for Distance Education: A Dropped Privacy Protection and New Transfer-Credit Disclosures Due by First Commitment
  8. Cal State Faculty Take AI to the Bargaining Table: Strike-Authorization Vote Closes November 19, With the $13 Million ChatGPT Deal in the Background
  9. Arizona Loses 5,280 Students in a Year and Iowa's Regents Brace for a 9 Percent Drop in Graduates, as State Systems Post Their First Declines in a Decade
  10. College Board: Net Tuition at Public Four-Year Colleges Is $1,920, Down From a $4,600 Peak, While Sticker Prices Pass $12,000
  11. Maryland Launches an Online Master of Public Health in Health Literacy at the In-State Rate for Every Student
  12. CPT Injunction Hearing Held as the $70,000 OPT Fee Comment Period Closes Monday
  13. Federal Register, November 5: Accreditors Up for Recognition Review, and Proposed Grant Priorities Naming Career Pathways and AI
  14. Maine Offers Buyouts to 158 Faculty to Close a $19 Million Gap; Miami University Lands a $100 Million Business School Gift
  15. McGraw Hill's Higher Ed Revenue Is Flat at $213.5 Million While Its AI Reader Passes 80 Million Interactions
  16. Competitor Spotlight: Purdue Global and UMGC; ASU Online and SNHU

One thing to watch: Repeal of the loan caps is off the table; the live mechanism is reclassifying nursing and allied health as professional degrees, and November 18 is the first oversight deadline.

item.title: SPECIAL EDITION — Redesigning Assessment for the AI Era
item.description:
Special edition. A practical overview of six strategies for making assessment in online courses resilient to generative AI, drawn from about 120 scholarly, institutional and practitioner sources published November 2025 through November 2026, plus a look at how institutions are funding faculty to redesign. Companion to the written research brief, "AI-Resistant Assessment Research Brief" (Penn State World Campus, November 6, 2026).

In this episode

  1. The problem: near-universal use, failed detection, and AI agents inside the LMS
  2. Strategy 1 — Verification conversations: live, unscripted dialogue about the student's own work
  3. Strategy 2 — Paired-evidence ("twin") designs: an open product linked to a secured component
  4. Strategy 3 — Program-level assurance mapping and the Australian quotas (Melbourne, Queensland, Sydney)
  5. Strategy 4 — Observed performance and workplace-attested practice
  6. Strategy 5 — Open-lane redesign: replacing discussion boards and quizzes, AI-integrated tasks that preserve learning
  7. Strategy 6 — Secured-assessment modernization: fewer, better, more accessible proctored hurdles
  8. Briefly: what no longer counts as assurance
  9. How institutions are paying for redesign — SUNY, Kansas, Michigan, Virginia Tech, Penn State's AI Center of Excellence
  10. One thing to watch — framing the call around assurance of learning, and producing the evidence the sector lacks

One thing to watch: the framing decides what faculty propose. A call framed around cheating and detection produces "Defenders"; a call framed around assurance of learning produces design. The sector has frameworks everywhere and outcome evidence almost nowhere, so a funded cohort that measures whether the verified and open components of a course tell the same story about the same student would be a contribution in its own right.

Sources

The problem — use, grades, detection and agents

  • Widespread AI misuse means higher ed must rethink assessment (Chirikov, Smirnov and Kizilcec, Science) — Cornell Chronicle
  • Student Generative AI Survey 2026 — HEPI
  • Brown professor says students used AI to cheat — The Boston Globe
  • Trusting AI to detect AI? A systematic evaluation of AIGC detection tools — Computers & Education
  • Why AI Detection Fails for Academic Integrity — arXiv (Notre Dame)
  • AI Detector Guidelines, draft v1.3 — Penn State Academic Integrity
  • On the Insecurity of Keystroke-Based AI Authorship Detection — arXiv
  • The Next Wave of AI-Cheating Technology — The Chronicle of Higher Education
  • A.I. Agents Are Taking Entire Online Courses for Cheating Students — The New York Times (syndicated)
  • Agentic AI, Academic Integrity, and the Question We Are Avoiding — WCET Frontiers
  • Assessment Design Forum 2026 takeaways (Phillip Dawson) — University of Auckland

Verification conversations and oral assessment

  • The Return of the Oral Exam — The Chronicle of Higher Education
  • Why colleges are turning to oral exams to combat AI — AP via Fortune
  • Interactive Oral Assessment — Dublin City University

item.content:encoded:
Special edition. A practical overview of six strategies for making assessment in online courses resilient to generative AI, drawn from about 120 scholarly, institutional and practitioner sources published November 2025 through November 2026, plus a look at how institutions are funding faculty to redesign. Companion to the written research brief, "AI-Resistant Assessment Research Brief" (Penn State World Campus, November 6, 2026).

In this episode

  1. The problem: near-universal use, failed detection, and AI agents inside the LMS
  2. Strategy 1 — Verification conversations: live, unscripted dialogue about the student's own work
  3. Strategy 2 — Paired-evidence ("twin") designs: an open product linked to a secured component
  4. Strategy 3 — Program-level assurance mapping and the Australian quotas (Melbourne, Queensland, Sydney)
  5. Strategy 4 — Observed performance and workplace-attested practice
  6. Strategy 5 — Open-lane redesign: replacing discussion boards and quizzes, AI-integrated tasks that preserve learning
  7. Strategy 6 — Secured-assessment modernization: fewer, better, more accessible proctored hurdles
  8. Briefly: what no longer counts as assurance
  9. How institutions are paying for redesign — SUNY, Kansas, Michigan, Virginia Tech, Penn State's AI Center of Excellence
  10. One thing to watch — framing the call around assurance of learning, and producing the evidence the sector lacks

One thing to watch: the framing decides what faculty propose. A call framed around cheating and detection produces "Defenders"; a call framed around assurance of learning produces design. The sector has frameworks everywhere and outcome evidence almost nowhere, so a funded cohort that measures whether the verified and open components of a course tell the same story about the same student would be a contribution in its own right.

Sources

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Thursday, 5 November 2026
item.description:
Coverage window: Tuesday, November 3 through Thursday, November 5, 2026. 12 stories plus the Competitor Spotlight.

In this episode

  1. Democrats Win Congress and Sweep the States, and the Senate Appropriations Chair Who Protected Pell Loses
  2. Four Governorships Flip, Texas Regent Seats Come Into Play, and Wisconsin Voters Bar Race and Sex Preferences in Public Education
  3. Higher Education Groups Press the IRS to Withdraw a Rule That Could Revoke Tax Exemptions Over Race-Conscious Programs
  4. Harvard Wins Twice in Federal Court: Admissions-Data Suit Dismissed, Gino Loses on Summary Judgment
  5. Grand Canyon Education's Third Quarter: GCU Online Enrollment Up 7.1 Percent While Campus Enrollment Falls 4.1 Percent
  6. Harvard Study: AI-Written Peer Reviews Beat Human Reviews, but the Evidence Is Thin
  7. UT Austin Agrees to Pay About $4.2 Million for ChatGPT and Claude; About 18,000 Accounts Exist Against Roughly 145,000 Seats
  8. University of Kentucky Grants a Humanist Employee a Religious Exemption From Using AI
  9. Clearinghouse Detail: Computer Science Enrollment Down More Than 10 Percent at Every Level While Health Programs Grow
  10. Universities of Wisconsin Fall Enrollment Slips 0.7 Percent, With International Students Accounting for Nearly All of the Loss
  11. Enrollment Managers Make Retention and Adult Learners the Focus; IU Online Finds 11 Percent of Students Are Returning Stop-Outs
  12. Job Cuts Hit Tulsa, Seton Hall, Stockton and Jackson State; Oregon's Plan Gets More Specific
  13. Competitor Spotlight: ASU Online and UMGC; Purdue Global and SNHU

One thing to watch: Expect oversight hearings rather than loan-cap repeal, starting with whether the agencies now running Education Department functions can handle student aid.

Sources

Federal policy and politics

  • 5 Takeaways as Democrats Win Big in States, Congress — Inside Higher Ed
  • Democrats Vie to Take Back House Education Committee — Inside Higher Ed
  • Terms of university systems' regents to expire weeks after Hinojosa takes office — KCBD
  • Voters give split decision on constitutional amendments to limit governor's powers, DEI — Wisconsin Public Radio

Legal and civil rights

  • Proposal That Could Ax College Tax Exemptions Condemned — Inside Higher Ed
  • ACE, Higher Education Groups Urge IRS to Withdraw Rule — American Council on Education
  • US judge dismisses Trump administration's Harvard admissions probe case — KFGO (Reuters)
  • Judge rules against former Harvard business professor Francesca Gino in tenure case — GBH

Online learning and enrollment

  • Grand Canyon Education Third Quarter 2026 Results (8-K Exhibit 99.1) — SEC EDGAR
  • 3 Takeaways on Enrollment Management — Inside Higher Ed

AI in education

  • AI Article Review 'Better Than Humans at Their Best' — Inside Higher Ed
  • UT agreed to pay about $4.2 million for ChatGPT, Claude education services, contracts show — The Daily Texan
  • U of Kentucky Says Humanist Admin Exempt From AI — Inside Higher Ed
  • U of Kentucky grants employee religious exemption from AI use — Higher Ed Dive

Enrollment

  • Fall 2026 college enrollment holds nearly flat as community colleges grow and master's programs decline — American School & University
  • Fearing AI, young workers retrain for hands-on jobs — Hechinger Report
  • Universities of Wisconsin enrollment decreases slightly this fall — Wisconsin Public Radio

Institutional finance

  • Latest Job Cuts Impact Both Public and Private Campuses — Inside Higher Ed

Competitor Spotlight

  • Derrick Anderson named CEO of ASU EdPlus — ASU News
  • UMGC awarded $1.25 million grant for skills-first initiative — UMGC News
  • UMGC and Newstate University announce new transfer credit agreement — UMGC News

Higher Ed News Digest is published every Monday and Thursday.

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Monday, 2 November 2026
item.description:
Coverage window: Friday, October 30 through Monday, November 2, 2026. 15 stories plus the Competitor Spotlight.

In this episode

  1. Education Department Finalizes the Accreditation Overhaul, Rejecting a Phase-In and Tightening Transfer-Credit Rules
  2. Preliminary Fall Enrollment: Undergraduate Growth Slows to 0.6 Percent While Master's Falls 3.7 Percent in the First Year of Federal Loan Caps
  3. Dartmouth Provost Resigns After Faculty Review Finds Undisclosed AI Use in His Writing
  4. Cornell Rolls Out ChatGPT Edu, Claude and Gemini Campuswide, With Training Required First
  5. Faculty Survey: Nearly Nine in Ten Say AI Has Hurt Their Confidence in Student Work
  6. Dartmouth Student Survey: Half Think Peers Copy AI Text, 8 Percent Admit Doing It
  7. Coursera's Third Quarter: Udemy Merger Savings Ahead of Plan, but Normalized Revenue Is Down 3 Percent
  8. Penn State and Universities of Wisconsin Both Report Fall Declines Driven by International Students
  9. DOJ Makes First Arrests in FAFSA "Ghost Student" Fraud Under Operation Ghostbusters
  10. What Is at Stake for Higher Education in Tuesday's Midterms
  11. University of Oregon Plans to Close a $65 Million Structural Deficit by Closing 18 Graduate Programs
  12. Comments on the $70,000 OPT Fee Proposal Close November 9
  13. Canvas Roadmap: New Interface on by Default in Mid-2027, LTI 1.1 Retired in December 2027
  14. Class Action Says ED Is Refusing Closed-School Discharges for Former For-Profit Students
  15. Cornell Faculty Voting on No Confidence in University Leadership
  16. Competitor Spotlight: Purdue Global and UMGC; ASU Online and SNHU

One thing to watch: Master's enrollment fell 3.7 percent in the first year of the federal graduate-loan caps, and the preliminary data cannot yet say whether online programs were hit harder.

Sources

Policy and accreditation

  • Final accreditation rule sets the stage for system overhaul — Higher Ed Dive
  • Trump's Accreditation Overhaul Finalized — Inside Higher Ed

  • Fall 2026 International Student Economic Snapshot — NAFSA
  • ED Refuses to Discharge Eligible Student Debt, Lawsuit Claims — Inside Higher Ed

Enrollment and research

  • Penn State University Fall Enrollment Drops — ABC23
  • Universities of Wisconsin enrollment tops 164,500 students for fall 2026 — WIXX

AI

  • Dartmouth provost resigns after review finds undisclosed AI use — NHPR

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Thursday, 29 October 2026 (new format)
item.description:
Coverage window: Tuesday, October 27 through Thursday, October 29, 2026. 15 stories plus the Competitor Spotlight.

In this episode

  1. Master's Enrollment Falls 3.7 Percent in the First Fall Under Federal Graduate Loan Caps, Clearinghouse Preliminary Data Show
  2. Michigan's Public Universities Lose 5,223 Students, Dropping to Their Lowest Fall Total in at Least a Decade
  3. California Competes Counts 6.4 Million Working-Age Adults Without a Degree and Calls for More Online and Hybrid Options
  4. Dartmouth's Provost Resigns After a Faculty Review Used His Campus Claude Logs, Not AI Detectors, to Find Undisclosed AI Use
  5. Cornell and Iowa Move to Multi-Model Campus AI, Offering Claude Alongside ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot
  6. UNC-Chapel Hill Drops AI Scoring of Admissions Essays Because Student AI Use Made the Scores Meaningless
  7. D2L Adds Central Control of AI Knowledge Sources and a Shared Course-Content Repository
  8. Tuberville Tells Students to "Quit" Some Four-Year Universities; Alabama Ranks Third on the Earnings Premium
  9. Students Rate a Degree's Purpose Above Its Economic Return in a Vendor Survey
  10. New Dashboard Previews the Federal Earnings Test State by State: A 76 Percent National Premium, but Alaska Sits at 28
  11. McMahon Closes Her Speech Series at Vanderbilt, Calling the Administration's Settlements "Much-Needed Scrutiny"
  12. College Scorecard Drops Most Minority-Serving Institution Filters and Adds Seven-Year Earnings
  13. University of Providence Will Close; It Had Lost Authorization to Teach Online Students in Several States
  14. Pomona College Will Become the Parent of Claremont Graduate University, Which Plans to Grow Online and Certificate Offerings
  15. University of Oregon Plans Graduate Program Cuts and About 100 Administrative Layoffs to Close a $63 Million Deficit
  16. Competitor Spotlight: UMGC, SNHU, plus DeVry and GCU (not tracked); ASU Online and Purdue Global

One thing to watch: Master's enrollment fell 3.7 percent in the first fall under federal graduate loan caps; online master's portfolios should watch their spring starts rather than wait for January's final figures.

Sources

Enrollment and adult learners

  • Undergraduate enrollment inched up this fall, while master's dips 3.7% — Higher Ed Dive
  • Preliminary Enrollment Data Shows Slower Growth — Inside Higher Ed
  • Michigan public universities lost over 5,000 students in fall 2026 — Higher Ed Dive
  • University enrollment drops 2% in Michigan — Bridge Michigan
  • The Untapped Potential of Adult Learners — Inside Higher Ed

AI and edtech

  • Dartmouth Provost Resigns Over AI Use — Inside Higher Ed
  • Here's the Latest News on College Leadership — The Chronicle of Higher Education
  • Cornell to Offer Free ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini Access — Cornell Daily Sun
  • New UI branded AI set to be available in 2027 — The Daily Iowan
  • Claude AI now available to Emory community — Emory News

Perceptions and politics

  • Ala. Senator: Students Should "Quit" Some 4-Year Universities — Inside Higher Ed
  • 4 Lessons on What Makes a College Degree Worthwhile — Inside Higher Ed

Policy and politics

  • Dashboard Analyzes Credential Earnings Premiums by State — Inside Higher Ed
  • McMahon: "Institutional Decay" Compelled a Reckoning — Inside Higher Ed
  • Secretary McMahon Delivers Next 250 Higher Education Remarks at Vanderbilt University — U.S. Department of Education

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Monday, 26 October 2026
item.description:
Coverage window: Friday, October 23 through Monday, October 26, 2026, plus a few October 20-22 items not carried in the last edition. 14 topic summaries plus the Competitor Spotlight.

In this episode

  1. McMahon Tells the Sector to "Follow ASU's Example" in a Speech Delivered at Arizona State
  2. Undergraduate Certificates Fail the New Earnings Test at 29 Percent, Analysis Finds
  3. Pentagon Says 30 Universities Ended More Than 80 Foreign Partnerships After Its Audit Order
  4. Maine Projects a $19 Million Shortfall and Syracuse Opens an Administrative Portfolio Review
  5. Pitt Weighs Early Retirements, Chemeketa Cuts $5 Million, and Two Minnesota Colleges Share a Campus
  6. Instructure's Canvas Tiers Take Effect as Free AI Access Lapses; MCP Agent Integration Remains in Trial
  7. Aspiring Public-College Accreditor CPHE Makes Its First Decision, Approving Florida Polytechnic
  8. Proposed OPT Fee Meets a Body of Research Linking Skilled Immigrants to Innovation
  9. Supreme Court Leaves New Hampshire's Student-ID Voting Restriction in Place for the Midterms
  10. Ohio Court Blocks Attempt to Dissolve Antioch University's Board
  11. Bard Names Pace's Marvin Krislov President as TCU's Chancellor Resigns After 17 Months
  12. UPCEA CEO Robert Hansen to Retire in 2027
  13. Fort Hays State Closes Its Natural History Museum to Absorb a State Budget Cut
  14. Kalshi Plans Contracts on Admission Rates at 22 Selective Colleges
  15. Competitor Spotlight: ASU Online, Purdue Global, SNHU and UMGC (ASU Online's federal endorsement and Purdue Global's accreditor-program invitation; SNHU and UMGC quiet this fortnight)

One thing to watch: The Secretary's speech was both the biggest story and the sharpest argument: the part to plan around is the earnings machinery behind the praise for ASU, with the first formal test calculations due in early 2027.

Sources

Federal policy, accountability and the Education Secretary

  • US secretary of education visits ASU, praises affordability — ASU News

  • Breaking Down OPT and How It Affects the Economy — Inside Higher Ed
  • Here's the Latest News on Trump and Higher Ed — The Chronicle of Higher Education
  • N.H. Voters May Not Use Student IDs at Midterm Polls — Inside Higher Ed

Accreditation, leadership and governance

  • Aspiring Accreditor Approves First Institution — Inside Higher Ed
  • GW official submits public comments on proposed federal accreditation rule — GW Hatchet
  • Ohio court blocks dissolution of Antioch University's board — Higher Ed Dive
  • Judge Blocks Attempted Breakup of Antioch Board — Inside Higher Ed
  • Krislov to Succeed Embattled President at Bard — Inside Higher Ed
  • TCU Chancellor Resigns Abruptly — Inside Higher Ed
  • UPCEA CEO Robert J. Hansen to Retire in 2027; Board to Launch National Search for Successor — Higher Ed Dive

Institutional finance and market

  • University of Maine eyes $6M in budget cuts, including layoffs — Higher Ed Dive

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Thursday, 22 October 2026
item.description:
Coverage window: Tuesday, October 20 through Thursday, October 22, 2026, plus a few October 19 items not carried in the last edition. 11 topic summaries plus the Competitor Spotlight.

In this episode

  1. UNC-Chapel Hill Settles With the Trump Administration, Paying Nothing and Accepting Two Years of Reporting
  2. Justice Department Finds Ohio State's Medical School Discriminated in Admissions
  3. Education Department Bars a Cosmetology Accreditor From Adding Members Instead of Stripping Its Recognition
  4. Texas Opens Its Own Antitrust Probe of the ABA Council as the Justice Department's Deadline Arrives
  5. Administration Moves to Drop Appeals of Rulings Blocking the PSLF Employer Rule
  6. Emory Adds Claude for Education as Stanford Updates a Three-Vendor AI Platform
  7. Gallup–Lumina Survey: 48 Percent of Employers Expect Higher Education to Matter More Because of AI
  8. More Than 240 Cornell Faculty Say the University Failed a Student Who Alleges Gang Rape
  9. Anna Maria College Cancels Its Campus Auction; Bennington Reports an $18 Million Deficit
  10. A Wave of Sticker-Price Resets and Income-Based Free Tuition Reaches Residential Colleges
  11. Xavier of Louisiana Will Open the Nation's Fifth HBCU Medical School in 2027
  12. Competitor Spotlight: ASU Online, Purdue Global, SNHU and UMGC (ASU Online's California guaranteed-admission pathway; the other three quiet this fortnight)

One thing to watch: North Carolina's settlement was the biggest story, but the Education Department's handling of accreditors is the one worth planning time. Under Secretary Kent has overridden the advisory committee twice this year, each time choosing a growth limit over termination, and about 300 applications are frozen at one accreditor alone.

Sources

Federal policy, civil rights and student aid

  • UNC-Chapel Hill strikes bargain with Trump administration to end probes — Higher Ed Dive
  • Here's the Latest News on Trump and Higher Ed — The Chronicle of Higher Education

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Monday, 19 October 2026
item.description:
Coverage window: Friday, October 16 through Monday, October 19, 2026, plus a few October 14–15 items not carried in the last edition. 7 topic summaries plus the Competitor Spotlight.

In this episode

  1. Harvard Posts a $100 Million Surplus, With Federal Research Revenue Down About 20 Percent
  2. Southern Accreditor's Draft Standards Add an "Intellectual Pluralism" Requirement, and the AAUP Objects
  3. Justice Department Threatens an Antitrust Probe of the ABA Council Over Limits on Adjunct Law Faculty
  4. University of Oregon Weighs Cutting Graduate Programs in Humanities and Education to Close a $65 Million Gap
  5. Ithaca College Floats Collapsing Five Schools Into Three
  6. University of Tulsa Cuts Nearly 9 Percent of Its Staff, Mostly in Central Administration
  7. Federal Judge Declines to Block Trump's March Anti-DEI Order for Contractors
  8. Competitor Spotlight: ASU Online, Purdue Global, SNHU and UMGC (quiet this fortnight); Grand Canyon University's new law school

One thing to watch: Harvard was the biggest story, but accreditation is the one worth planning time. A regional accreditor, the Justice Department and the state of Arizona each moved on accreditor authority in the same week, with the Education Department's rule targeted for finalization around November 1.

Sources

Finance and institutional restructuring

  • Harvard logs $100M surplus despite 20% drop in federal research money — Higher Ed Dive
  • Harvard Stabilizes Finances With Strong Endowment Returns, Philanthropy — Harvard Magazine
  • Finance Live Updates — The Chronicle of Higher Education
  • UO weighing cuts to graduate programs in humanities, education — Lookout Eugene-Springfield
  • Ithaca College weighs three-school academic structure, says no plan is final — FingerLakes1
  • University of Tulsa to cut nearly 9 percent of its workforce — FOX23

Accreditation and federal policy

  • AAUP Opposes Accreditor's Intellectual Diversity Proposal — Inside Higher Ed
  • Justice Department threatens antitrust probe of ABA Legal Ed council over accreditation standards — ABA Journal
  • Judge declines to block Trump's March anti-DEI order for federal contractors — Higher Ed Dive

Competitor Spotlight

  • GCU to build Arizona's third law school after state Supreme Court approval — KOLD
  • GCU News — Grand Canyon University

Published twice weekly, Mondays and Thursdays.

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Thursday, 15 October 2026
item.description:
Coverage window: Tuesday, October 13 through Thursday, October 15, 2026. Thirteen stories plus the Competitor Spotlight.

In this episode

  1. Penn State Proposes Eliminating 47 Undergraduate Programs After a Multiyear Review
  2. A New Analysis Finds the Federal Earnings Test Will Touch About 2.5 Percent of Aid Recipients, Concentrated in Certificates and Online Graduate Mental Health Programs
  3. The Education Department Publishes Its College Affordability and Transparency Report, With Institutions' Answers Released as Data for the First Time
  4. Fifty-Six Congressional Democrats Condemn the Education Department's Transfer of Minority-Serving Institution Funds
  5. Minnesota State's Board Approves Redirecting Up to $25 Million a Year to Struggling Colleges
  6. Five Independent Colleges Join a New Accreditor as Founding Members
  7. Newcastle and Westminster Decline to Renew Turnitin, Joining Southampton
  8. Arizona State Launches an Intel-Funded AI Computing Platform for Students and Researchers
  9. A Consultancy Poll Finds 34 Percent of Students Ruled Out a College Solely Over Its State's Politics
  10. ACT: One in Three of the Class of 2026 Retook the Exam, Gaining 1.1 Points on Average
  11. Knight–Ipsos: 37 Percent of College Students Feel Free Speech Is Secure, Down From 73 Percent in 2016
  12. MacKenzie Scott Gives 10,000 Degrees an Unrestricted $42 Million, Its Largest Gift
  13. New College of Florida Becomes the First Known Institution to Opt In to the State's Armed Guardian Program
  14. Competitor Spotlight: ASU Online, Purdue Global, SNHU and UMGC

One thing to watch: The biggest story was Penn State's 47-program proposal, but the one worth planning time is the earnings test: about 2.5 percent of aid recipients are in programs expected to fail, concentrated in certificates and graduate mental health programs, where the largest are at largely online institutions. Penalties cannot begin before 2028.

Sources

Programs, Finance and Governance

  • Penn State looks to cut 47 undergraduate degrees — Higher Ed Dive
  • Minnesota State board approves plan to redirect funding to struggling colleges — Higher Ed Dive
  • 5 Independent Colleges Sign Up for New Accreditor — Inside Higher Ed

Federal and State Policy

  • New Earnings Test Will Have Limited but Concentrated Impact — Inside Higher Ed
  • Release of the College Affordability and Transparency Report — Federal Student Aid
  • Congressional Democrats Condemn MSI Funding Transfer — Inside Higher Ed
  • ED Redirects $235M in MSI Funds to HBCUs, Tribal Colleges — Inside Higher Ed
  • At Least One College Opts In to Florida's Armed Guardian Program — Inside Higher Ed

Edtech

  • More U.K. Universities End Turnitin Contracts — Inside Higher Ed
  • More universities end Turnitin contracts as concerns mount — Times Higher Education
  • ASU provides access to AI-supercomputing for all — ASU News

Enrollment, Students and Philanthropy

  • More students are ruling out colleges based on politics, poll finds — Higher Ed Dive
  • 1 in 3 ACT test-takers retook the exam — and raised their scores — Higher Ed Dive
  • Survey: Majority of College Students Say Free Speech Threatened — Inside Higher Ed
  • Expanding College Success for Low-Income Students — Inside Higher Ed

Competitor Spotlight

  • No significant activity in the competitor landscape this fortnight.

Published twice weekly, Mondays and Thursdays.

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Monday, 12 October 2026
item.description:
Coverage window: Friday, October 9 through Monday, October 12, 2026. Fourteen stories plus the Competitor Spotlight.

In this episode

  1. Nine Universities Are Subpoenaed in a Labor Department Inquiry Into J-1 Visa Use
  2. Three Are Indicted Over an Alleged $20 Million Scheme at Now-Closed Eastern Gateway Community College
  3. More Than 1,000 Colleges Missed the Deadline to Submit Student Outcomes Data
  4. 93 Percent of Programs Pass the New Federal Earnings Test, but Only 82 Percent Pass a Stricter Value Benchmark
  5. The Education Department's Research Arm Obligated 99.5 Percent of Its Budget After a Late-September Surge
  6. CU Denver Plans the First U.S. Public University Branch Campus in India, With Emeritus as Partner
  7. NACAC Attendees Worry Less About AI Essays Than About AI College Search, and More Americans Consider Study Abroad
  8. Texas Universities Extend Guaranteed Tuition to Middle-Income Families
  9. Stockton University Plans 21 Layoffs Amid a Deficit Above $20 Million
  10. Valley Forge Military College Weighs Leaving Pennsylvania as Oklahoma Courts It
  11. Education Department Expands Its Antisemitism Investigation at Swarthmore
  12. Judge Dismisses Race Bias and Retaliation Claims by Purdue Fort Wayne's Former Chief Diversity Officer
  13. A Vendor Launch and a Survey Point to the Same AI Governance Gap: Policies Without Enforcement
  14. Daytona College Co-Owner Dies After an Attack; a Contractor Is Charged With Murder
  15. Competitor Spotlight: ASU Online, Purdue Global, SNHU and UMGC

One thing to watch: The biggest story was the J-1 subpoenas, but the one worth planning time is the outcomes-data deadline: more than 1,000 colleges missed the October 1 submission, and failing to submit properly by January 15, 2027 could cost an institution access to federal grants and loans.

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Thursday, 8 October 2026
item.description:
Coverage window: Tuesday, October 6 through Thursday, October 8, 2026. Sixteen stories plus the Competitor Spotlight.

In this episode

  1. DHS Proposes a $70,000 Fee for Colleges to Recommend Students for OPT
  2. Four Higher Ed Groups Sue DHS Over Restrictions on Curricular Practical Training
  3. Harvard Argues Twice at the First Circuit Over Research Funding and International Enrollment
  4. Third Circuit Vacates the Ruling That Ordered Penn to Disclose Jewish Employees' Names
  5. Judge Dismisses DOJ Challenge to Virginia's In-State Tuition for Undocumented Students
  6. Lincoln University Students and Alumni Sue Missouri for $548.7 Million in Underfunding
  7. As the Cohort Default Rate Stays Near Zero, Other Education Department Data Points the Other Way
  8. Tennessee Becomes the Fifth State to Move Beyond ABA Accreditation for Law Schools
  9. Antioch's Fight With Its Parent Coalition Reaches the Accreditor
  10. September Brought Large Layoffs, Led by Utah's Plan to Cut Up to 855 Positions
  11. Minnesota State Community and Technical College Plans to Close Its Detroit Lakes Campus
  12. Utah's Technical Colleges Have 8,055 People on Wait Lists
  13. University of Maryland's Randomized Trial of Its AI Study Assistant Leaves the Rollout on Hold
  14. OpenAI Will Retire Custom GPTs on December 11 and Introduces Persistent Dots Agents
  15. Amazon Pledges Free Community College for Residents of Its Data Center Communities
  16. University of Houston-Downtown Tests a Comprehensive Model for Bringing Back Stopped-Out Students
  17. Competitor Spotlight: ASU Online, Purdue Global, SNHU and UMGC

One thing to watch: The biggest story was the OPT fee, but the one worth planning time is the 0.4 percent national cohort default rate, a figure the Education Department itself says may be overly favorable, set against 9.3 million borrowers in default.

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Thursday, 1 October 2026
item.description:
Coverage window: Tuesday, September 29 through Thursday, October 1, 2026. Eleven stories plus the Competitor Spotlight.

In this episode

  1. Carnegie Mellon Lands a $3 Billion Gift From Ken Griffin, the Largest Individual Gift in Higher Education History
  2. Education Department Formally Rescinds the 2024 Title IX Rule Without Notice and Comment
  3. An $810 Million Pocket Rescission Puts $70 Million in International Education Funding at Risk
  4. Colleges Prepare Financial Aid Systems to Administer Workforce Pell as the Department Approves Programs
  5. Instructure Data: The Top Dedicated AI Tool in Canvas Ranks Outside the Top 100 Integrations
  6. Antioch-Otterbein Coalition Fractures in Court as Antioch's Board Loses Its Injunction Bid
  7. Valencia, South Carolina State and Fort Hays State Cut Programs and a Museum Under Budget Pressure
  8. Oakland City University Resigns Its Higher Learning Commission Accreditation
  9. Senate Passes the Protect College Sports Act, 77-22
  10. WCET Analysis: The New Federal Distance Education Definition and Modality Reporting
  11. Newsom Vetoes Bill Requiring CSU Reports on Protest-Related Student Discipline
  12. Competitor Spotlight: ASU Online, Purdue Global, SNHU and UMGC

One thing to watch: The biggest story was Carnegie Mellon's $3 billion gift, but the one worth planning time is Instructure's Canvas data: the top dedicated AI tool reaches 87,788 of 19.5 million users, so AI licenses are not yet being embedded in courses.

Sources

Philanthropy

  • Carnegie Mellon University Announces Historic $3 Billion Gift from Ken Griffin — Carnegie Mellon University

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Monday, 28 September 2026
item.description:
Coverage window: Friday, September 25 through Monday, September 28, 2026. Ten stories plus the Competitor Spotlight.

In this episode

  1. Visa Scrutiny Knocks Double-Digit Percentages Off International Enrollment at Five Public Systems
  2. NACIQI Recommends Suspending APA's Accreditor Over Antisemitism Complaints, Punts on the ABA Again
  3. Forty Higher-Ed Groups Object to an Education Department Rule Expanding Grant-Termination Power
  4. University of Minnesota Moves to Two-Year Budgeting to Absorb $225 Million in Cuts
  5. Bowie State Cuts Twenty More Faculty as Its Deficit Stretches Into 2028
  6. UT Austin Approves Sixteen of Forty-Nine Core Curriculum Proposals, None From Women's and Gender Studies
  7. Developer Indicted for Defrauding Allen University of Millions in a Stadium Deal Gone Bad
  8. Dartmouth Opens a Review After Its Provost's Anti-AI Op-Ed Turns Out to Be Mostly AI
  9. Faculty Developers Make the Case for Abandoning the AI-Proofing Arms Race
  10. Alabama's Community College System Takes AI Literacy Training on the Road
  11. Competitor Spotlight: ASU Online, Purdue Global, SNHU and UMGC

One thing to watch: Visa scrutiny is compressing international enrollment at flagship public systems, but the same scrutiny is a variable, not a constant, for a national online enterprise — the real number to watch is whether online international enrollment moves at all over the next two admissions cycles.

Sources

International Enrollment

  • Major public universities report hits to international enrollment — Higher Ed Dive

Accreditation and Policy

  • Accreditation panel recommends suspending APA, punts on ABA — Inside Higher Ed
  • Higher-ed groups bash ED proposal to allow more grant terminations — Inside Higher Ed
  • UT Austin cuts women's and gender studies courses from core — Inside Higher Ed

Institutional Finance

  • University of Minnesota plans $225 million in budget cuts over two years — MPR News
  • University of Minnesota eyes $225M in budget cuts — Higher Ed Dive
  • Bowie State University layoffs — The Baltimore Banner

Legal and Leadership

  • Developer indicted for defrauding Allen University — Inside Higher Ed
  • Beilock announces committee-led review of Provost Santiago Schnell's AI use — The Dartmouth
  • Dartmouth's provost quietly used AI in his published work — The Chronicle of Higher Education

AI and Edtech

  • Stop trying to AI-proof your assignments — eCampus News
  • Alabama Community College System brings AI literacy training to Enterprise — WTVY

Competitor Spotlight

  • No new sources — ASU Online, Purdue Global, SNHU and UMGC were quiet for a third consecutive edition.

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Thursday, 24 September 2026
item.description:
Coverage window: Wednesday, September 23 through Thursday, September 24, 2026. Ten stories plus the Competitor Spotlight.

In this episode

  1. A Federal Panel Talks Itself to a Standstill on Whether Law Schools Keep Their Accreditor
  2. DOJ Finds UCSF Medical School Discriminated by Twelve-to-One Against White Applicants, and It's the Fifth UC Campus Accused
  3. The Education Department Moves $235 Million From Hispanic-Serving Grants to HBCUs and Tribal Colleges, Again
  4. Iowa's GOP-Built Civics Center Loses Nearly Half Its Outside Advisers in a Day
  5. The Knights Give Oregon a Billion Dollars for Engineering While the University Plans $65 Million in Cuts
  6. Commonwealth University Weighs 175 Cuts as Pennsylvania Moves to Require Public Notice Before Closures
  7. Central Connecticut's President Resigns After a Bullying Complaint Ends the Investigation Before It Starts
  8. A16z Launches an Unaccredited Two-Year Alternative to College, Backed by Every Major AI Lab
  9. Penn Engineering Merges Its AI and Data Science Tracks Into One Master's Degree
  10. Provosts Use AI Weekly Themselves. Only One in Ten Institutions Has a Strategy For It.
  11. Competitor Spotlight: ASU Online, Purdue Global, SNHU and UMGC

One thing to watch: Andreessen Horowitz's new unaccredited "AI Academy" skips the credential entirely and sells network access to the biggest AI labs instead — aimed at exactly the career-motivated student that online degree programs also compete for.

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Tuesday, 22 September 2026
item.description:
Covering Monday evening, September 21 through Tuesday, September 22, 2026 — 13 topic summaries plus the standing Competitor Spotlight. An unusually short window: the previous edition ran Monday, September 21, so this edition reflects a single news day.

In this episode

  1. U.S. News Drops Graduate Debt for Graduate Earnings, and MIT Takes the Top Spot
  2. Labor Department Guidance Opens an Apprenticeship Fast Track Around the Workforce Pell Bottleneck
  3. Accreditation Comment Docket Closes at More Than 4,590, and the Sector's Own Associations Say the Rule Breaks the HEA
  4. Federal Research Grantmaking Enters the Final Week of the Fiscal Year Far Behind Pace
  5. Census Bureau Economists Find AI-Exposed Majors Graduating Into Recession-Scale Earnings Losses
  6. Austin Community College Builds a "Digital Twin" for 46,000 Students on an $875,000 Grant
  7. The Sterling College Post-Mortem Names the Online Pivot It Declined to Make
  8. Justice Department Cross-Moves for Summary Judgment in the Maryland DREAM Act Case
  9. Newsom Vetoes Campus Employment Bill for Undocumented Students a Second Time
  10. First Full Year of Federally Mandated Hazing Disclosures: 556 Incidents, and Barely Half of Campuses Complied
  11. Two Workforce Studies Point the Same Direction: AI Fluency Is Leaving the Technical Majors
  12. Gartner: For Every Dollar Spent on Generative AI Models, Fifty-Two Go to Infrastructure
  13. Students Are Not Technophobic About AI; They Are Uneasy About the Relationship
  14. Competitor Spotlight: ASU Online, Purdue Global, SNHU and UMGC

One thing to watch: The biggest story was the U.S. News release, but the one worth your planning time is the Labor Department's apprenticeship bulletin — and specifically the instructional outsourcing ceiling nobody quoted: 49% for an apprenticeship-partnered Workforce Pell program against 25% for everything else. That is a standing federal preference, written into eligibility, for a delivery model in which a substantial share of instruction sits outside the institution — which is a design question for any national online enterprise, not a compliance detail.

Rankings and methodology

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Monday, 21 September 2026
item.description:
Covering Friday, September 18 through Monday, September 21, 2026 — 16 topic summaries plus the Competitor Spotlight.

In this episode

  1. Workforce Pell Is Eighty-Two Days Old and Has Five Approved Programs Nationwide
  2. Comments Close on the Accreditation Overhaul, and Accreditors Spent the Weekend Filing Against It
  3. Two Judges Rule the Administration's Funding Maneuvers Illegal as a Billion Sits Unspent Nine Days From the Fiscal Cliff
  4. Two Fronts Open on NIH Grantmaking: A Keyword Lawsuit and a Draft Executive Order
  5. The New Loan Caps Are Stranding Seniors Mid-Degree While the Department's Guidance Keeps Moving
  6. California Opens Community College Bachelor's Degrees to Direct Competition With CSU and UC
  7. A Global Academic Freedom Count, and a Campus Speech Case That Collapsed Under Its Own Weight
  8. A New Report Argues AI Procurement, Not AI Cheating, Is the Unguarded Risk
  9. Google Turns Its Own AI Product Training Into Accredited College Credit
  10. The Post-OPM Market Consolidates: Risepoint Absorbs Keypath, Carnegie Hires Todd Zipper
  11. Sydney Launches a Library-Model Lending Platform for Commercial Video Games, and Stanford Signs On
  12. Penn State Will Sell Two of the Seven Commonwealth Campuses It Is Closing
  13. Maine Faces Retrenchment on a $19 Million Gap; Fitch Downgrades Xavier
  14. A Donor-Intent Report Finds Universities Can Rewrite Gift Agreements With Near Impunity
  15. Clearinghouse Benchmarks: Low-Income College-Going Rises, and the Straight-to-College Gap Holds at 22.7 Points
  16. The Campus Visit Becomes a Budget Line, and It Is the One Channel Online Cannot Copy
  17. Competitor Spotlight: ASU Online, Purdue Global, SNHU and UMGC

One thing to watch: Workforce Pell's slow start is not the story — the architecture is. A program is only eligible where a governor has approved it, so a national provider faces a fifty-state permitting problem rather than one federal approval, and the states have not converged. The provision almost nobody is discussing: eligibility depends on placing 70 percent of completers in jobs, measured through state employment data, and a completer who takes a job in another state is counted not as placed elsewhere but as not placed. Recruiting beyond your own state's labor market degrades the number that decides whether your program survives.

  5. The New Loan Caps Are Stranding Seniors Mid-Degree While the Department's Guidance Keeps Moving
  6. California Opens Community College Bachelor's Degrees to Direct Competition With CSU and UC
  7. A Global Academic Freedom Count, and a Campus Speech Case That Collapsed Under Its Own Weight
  8. A New Report Argues AI Procurement, Not AI Cheating, Is the Unguarded Risk
  9. Google Turns Its Own AI Product Training Into Accredited College Credit
  10. The Post-OPM Market Consolidates: Risepoint Absorbs Keypath, Carnegie Hires Todd Zipper
  11. Sydney Launches a Library-Model Lending Platform for Commercial Video Games, and Stanford Signs On

  16. The Campus Visit Becomes a Budget Line, and It Is the One Channel Online Cannot Copy

One thing to watch: Workforce Pell's slow start is not the story — the architecture is. A program is only eligible where a governor has approved it, so a national provider faces a fifty-state permitting problem rather than one federal approval, and the states have not converged. The provision almost nobody is discussing: eligibility depends on placing 70 percent of completers in jobs, measured through state employment data, and a completer who takes a job in another state is counted not as placed elsewhere but as not placed. Recruiting beyond your own state's labor market degrades the number that decides whether your program survives.

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Thursday, 17 September 2026
item.description:
Covering Tuesday, September 15 through Thursday, September 17, 2026 — 16 topic summaries plus the Competitor Spotlight.

In this episode

  1. A Judge Blocks the Four-Year Visa Cap One Day Before It Took Effect
  2. Education and State Departments Open Foreign-Funding Investigations Into Duke and North Dakota
  3. Presidents Expect the Accreditation Overhaul to Change Almost Nothing, With Comments Closing Monday
  4. Plaintiffs Say the Education Department Is Withholding 1,300 Records About Its Own Layoffs
  5. Asbury Theological Seminary Will Stop Taking Federal Loans as the Earnings Test Bites
  6. Perdoceo Buys South University in a Deal Worth Up to $224 Million
  7. Court Orders Antioch and the Coalition It Co-Founded Into Mediation
  8. UPCEA: AI-Generated Answers Now Decide Which Online Programs Make the Shortlist
  9. Two in Three Harvard Faculty Say AI Has Hurt Their Courses, Up From 42 Percent
  10. Elon Survey: Heavy AI Use, Deep Distrust, and Colleges Rated the Most Credible Guide
  11. Fall Census Numbers Keep Landing, and Online Is Where the Growth Is
  12. Forty-Two of 101 HBCUs Have Grown Since 2019, and Growth Is Its Own Problem
  13. Carleton Goes No-Loan on $80 Million in Gifts, and Needs $48 Million More
  14. USC Cuts 65 More From Engineering; Hartford Trims $7 Million
  15. Legacy Preferences Have Halved in a Decade but Held at the Most Selective
  16. Academic Freedom: A Kentucky Senator's Email and a Sixteen-Month Suspension in Texas
  17. Competitor Spotlight: ASU Online, Purdue Global, SNHU and UMGC

One thing to watch: Judge Saylor did not rule that a four-year cap on student visas is unlawful — he ruled that DHS built this one badly, on procedural grounds that are curable, and the curricular practical training restrictions from the same rulemaking were left standing and are in force right now.

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Monday, 14 September 2026
item.description:
Covering Friday, September 11 through Monday, September 14, 2026 — 16 topic summaries plus the Competitor Spotlight.

In this episode

  1. The Research Behind the Campus AI Buying Wave Barely Exists
  2. Sydney Signs With OpenAI a Week After Its Staff Struck Over AI
  3. Indiana University Quietly Cuts ChatGPT Edu Credits by More Than Eighty Percent
  4. A Philosophy Journal Published a Paper Written Largely by Claude
  5. Moody's: Stripping Tax Exemption Would Hit Fundraising First and Borrowing Hardest
  6. House Democrats Would Give Colleges the Same IRS Protections Churches Have
  7. The Accreditation Overhaul Comment Period Closes September 21
  8. Duration of Status Ends Tuesday, With Still No Ruling From the Bench
  9. Justice and Education Find Berkeley Law Violated Title VI
  10. NSF Opens $1.5 Billion Under a New Portfolio Model for Grant-Making
  11. Utah Will Shed Somewhere Between 285 and 855 Staff
  12. Cuts at Three More Campuses, and One Genuine Turnaround
  13. Temple Walks Away From the Largest Gift in Its History
  14. ACE: Eighty-Five Percent of Presidents Say Policy Chaos Has Degraded Their Aid Offers
  15. Next Week's U.S. News Rankings Carry Two Methodology Changes at Once
  16. The Presidential Churn Keeps Moving
  17. Illinois Scales Its Online Dual Credit Program to Twenty-One High Schools
  18. Competitor Spotlight: ASU Online, Purdue Global, SNHU and UMGC

One thing to watch: Indiana University cut its ChatGPT Edu allowance by more than 80 percent on September 1, eight months into OpenAI's second-largest education deployment — so the first constraint to arrive on campus AI was not pedagogical but metered, and a license you have to ration is a license you cannot build required coursework on.

Sources

AI, edtech and online learning

  • The "Nonexistent" Research on AI's Benefits for Education — Inside Higher Ed
  • UITS changes ChatGPT Edu policy, limits advanced features — Indiana Daily Student
  • USyd signs multi-year partnership with OpenAI — Honi Soit
  • UNSW partners with OpenAI — UNSW Newsroom
  • From classrooms to newsrooms: OpenAI expands initiatives to support journalism — EdTech Innovation Hub
  • Collaboration or Cheating? The Debate Over AI Use Is Dividing Scholars — The Chronicle of Higher Education
  • The Ivy League's Surrender to AI Is Insane — The Chronicle of Higher Education
  • Illinois announces tie-ups with 21 high schools for dual-credit initiative — EdTech Innovation Hub

Federal and state policy, legal and accreditation

  • Reps. Adams, Raskin Introduce HONEST Act — Office of Rep. Alma Adams
  • Accreditation, Innovation and Modernization: The Secretary's Recognition of Accrediting Agencies — Federal Register
  • Last Chance to Comment: ED Releases Proposed Rule on Accreditation Regulations — Higher Learning Commission
  • Joint Investigation Finds UC Berkeley Law Violated Title VI — U.S. Department of Justice
  • The colleges facing DOJ accusations of racial discrimination in admissions — Higher Ed Dive
  • NSF announces $1.5B for foundational research — National Science Foundation

International enrollment

  • Duration of Status Legal Defense — NAFSA
  • Duration of Status Litigation — Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration

Institutional finance, enrollment and leadership

  • IRS tax plan could imperil college finances, Moody's says — Higher Ed Dive
  • University of Utah could cut up to 15% of staff — Higher Ed Dive
  • University of Utah continues modernization effort — University of Utah
  • Here's the Latest News on Campus Finance — The Chronicle of Higher Education
  • Here's the Latest News on Campus Leadership — The Chronicle of Higher Education
  • Twelve staff members laid off ahead of the fall semester — The Berkeley Beacon
  • GW Law lays off personnel amid financial challenges, dean confirms — The GW Hatchet
  • Golden Gate University sells San Francisco skyscraper — SFGATE
  • Temple University cancels record $55M gift as donor faces fraud allegations — Higher Ed Dive
  • Temple University Ends $55 Million Gift by Trustee Who's Under Investigation — Forbes
  • Pulse Point Survey, Fall 2026 — American Council on Education
  • Coming Soon: 2027 Best Colleges With New Earnings Metric — U.S. News & World Report
  • Clemson texts reveal anxious courtship of would-be president — The Post and Courier

Competitor Spotlight

  • Purdue Global's School of Nursing expands access to education and workforce development — Purdue Global Newsroom

The Higher Ed News Digest publishes twice weekly, on Mondays and Thursdays.

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Thursday, 10 September 2026
item.description:
Coverage window: Tuesday, September 8 through Thursday, September 10, 2026 — 16 topic summaries plus the standing Competitor Spotlight.

In this episode

  1. An Accreditor Repeals Its Diversity Standard While Its Federal Recognition Hangs in the Balance
  2. Duration-of-Status Rule Takes Effect September 15 With Still No Ruling From the Bench
  3. Education Department Puts Central Arkansas Under Two Years of Monitoring Over Scholarships
  4. Democrats Say a Pentagon Agreement Would Divert Up to $2 Billion From NIH Research
  5. New Federal Loan Rules Delayed Summer Disbursements, and the Fall Risk Has Not Passed
  6. California Passes Community College Bachelor's Bills, and Both Systems Switched Sides
  7. Education Department Clears Bay Path's Acquisition of Cambridge College After Two and a Half Years
  8. Idaho's Departing President Calls the Failed University of Phoenix Purchase a Lost Opportunity
  9. Four Presidents Out and Two Under Investigation in Forty-Eight Hours
  10. Humanities Degrees Fall to Their Lowest Count Since 1991
  11. Fall 2026 Census Numbers Split Sharply Between Flagships and Regionals
  12. Applications to AI-Exposed Degrees Keep Rising as Entry-Level Jobs in Those Fields Shrink
  13. UNESCO Digital Learning Week Produces a Ministerial Statement on AI in Education
  14. Boise State Publishes Its Own Cut of a 45,000-Response Global AI Survey
  15. AI Moves From Support Tool Into the Delivery Layer, and Staff Push Back
  16. Campus Space Is Still Half Empty, According to the Firm That Sells the Occupancy Sensors
  17. Competitor Spotlight: ASU Online, Purdue Global, SNHU and UMGC

One thing to watch: a federally recognized accreditor repealed a substantive standard sixteen days before the committee that decides whether it keeps that recognition convenes — and its own members said on the record that survival was the reason. Comments on the Education Department's 354-page accreditation rule close September 21; NACIQI meets September 23.

Sources

Accreditation and federal enforcement

  • Colleges are scrambling to figure out new student loan rules. Students are paying the price — The Hechinger Report
  • College loans were late due to new federal rules — The Washington Post

International enrollment

  • Legal Challenge to the Final Rule Ending Duration of Status — NAFSA
  • Duration of Status Litigation — Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration

Institutions, finance and leadership

  • ED Approves Bay Path Acquisition of Cambridge College — Inside Higher Ed

  • Green to step down as U of I president — Idaho Education News
  • After a 2-Year Courtship, the U. of Idaho Calls Off Pursuit of the U. of Phoenix — The Chronicle of Higher Education
  • Here's the Latest News on Campus Leadership — The Chronicle of Higher Education
  • Colleges improve on utilization of classroom, office space — Higher Ed Dive

Enrollment and market research

  • Humanities degrees hit their lowest numbers in decades — Higher Ed Dive
  • Bachelor's Degrees in the Humanities — American Academy of Arts & Sciences
  • U of I breaks enrollment record with largest freshman class ever — University of Illinois News Bureau
  • NIU fall 2026 enrollment down 1.7% from last year — Northern Public Radio

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Monday, 7 September 2026
item.description:
Covering Friday, September 4 through Monday, September 7, 2026 — 15 stories plus the Competitor Spotlight.

In this episode

  1. Treasury and IRS Move to Strip Tax-Exempt Status From Colleges With Race-Conscious Policies
  2. Florida Bars Undocumented Students From Its Selective Public Universities
  3. House Passes Bill Cutting Federal Aid to Colleges That Boycott Israel
  4. Bipartisan Bill Would Block the Outsourcing of Four Education Department Offices
  5. Continuing Resolution Freezes the OMB Grants Rule Until Mid-December
  6. Middle States Quits C-RAC as the Accreditation Comment Deadline Nears
  7. No Ruling Yet on Duration of Status, and DHS Quietly Narrows Internship Eligibility
  8. Washington Pays a Professor $600,000 Over a Parody Land Acknowledgment
  9. Meredith College Has Lost More Than a Fifth of Its Faculty in a Year
  10. EAB: Student Need Is Rising Just as Capacity to Meet It Falls
  11. Texas Has Become the Sector's Contested Recruiting Ground
  12. U.S. News Will Add an Earnings by Major Metric on September 22
  13. Michigan State Opens AI Curriculum to Every Major on a $5 Million Anonymous Gift
  14. Wyoming Picks a Multi-Model Broker as Its Enterprise AI Platform
  15. WCET Makes the Case That AI Should Push Universities From Knowing to Being
  16. Competitor Spotlight: ASU Online, Purdue Global, SNHU, UMGC

One thing to watch: Revoking 501(c)(3) status would make private colleges owe federal income tax and end the deductibility of gifts — about $24 billion a year, roughly 8 percent of private nonprofit college revenue. The rule's exemptions preserve income, geography, first-generation, hardship and military-family criteria, so the adult-learner playbook sits inside the safe harbor while identity-linked scholarships do not.

item.title: Higher Ed News Digest — Monday, 31 August 2026
item.description:
Covering Friday 28 August through Monday 31 August 2026, plus several late-week stories the previous edition did not reach. Thirteen reports, leading with MIT's conclusion that AI can already complete almost any undergraduate written assignment.

In this episode

  1. MIT says AI can already complete "almost any" undergraduate written assignment
  2. Judge rules Rubio's revocation of pro-Palestinian students' visas unconstitutional
  3. ICE tightens Curricular Practical Training; UCLA and Berkeley pause processing
  4. Justice Department finds race discrimination at George Washington's medical school
  5. Florida moves to regulate AI from pre-K through its 12 public universities
  6. House Rules Committee takes up campus boycott funding bill
  7. Texas governor orders a working group on three-year bachelor's degrees
  8. Twenty Michigan colleges launch a direct admissions portal
  9. NBER: Tennessee Promise raised enrollment and attainment at under $1,000 a student
  10. Grand Canyon University adds a law school and a construction technology college
  11. PayPal and Venmo enter the campus tuition payments business
  12. Neighbor's right-of-first-refusal claim complicates Anna Maria's bankruptcy sale
  13. Saint Augustine's wins a stay on former trustees' legal costs
  14. Competitor Spotlight: ASU Online, UMGC, Purdue Global, SNHU

One thing to watch: the significant part of the MIT report is not that AI can pass undergraduate written work — anyone teaching this year already knows that. It is the buried request that curriculum changes made in response to AI be allowed to bypass "fixed, multi-committee, year-long review processes." That is a governance recommendation, not a pedagogy one, and every faculty senate in the country is about to receive some version of it.

Sources

AI, assessment and campus technology

  • AI can complete 'almost' all written assignments for MIT undergrads, report says — Higher Ed Dive
  • MIT AI Report Calls for Alternative Grading, Social Learning — Inside Higher Ed
  • DeSantis administration moving to regulate AI from pre-K to Ph.D. — Florida Phoenix
  • Some colleges begin accepting tuition payments via Venmo — Higher Ed Dive

Courts, civil rights and federal enforcement

  • Judge Rules Rubio's Efforts to Deport Students Violated Their Right to Free Speech — NOTUS
  • Trump admin unjustly revoked pro-Palestinian foreign students' visas, judge finds — The Hill
  • Trump administration seeks to restrict internships for international students — CP24
  • Justice Department Finds George Washington University Medical School Discriminates Based on Race in Admissions — U.S. Department of Justice
  • DOJ Finds Racial Discrimination at George Washington U Medical School — Inside Higher Ed

Federal and state policy

  • H.R. 4795 — Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act of 2026 — House Rules Committee
  • Meeting announcement for August 31, 2026 — House Rules Committee
  • Texas governor pushes for 3-year degree pathways — Higher Ed Dive

Admissions, enrollment and access research

  • 20 Michigan colleges join new direct admissions program — Higher Ed Dive
  • Tennessee Promise Boosts College Enrollment and Attainment, Data Shows — Inside Higher Ed
  • Working Paper 35226: Tennessee Promise — National Bureau of Economic Research

Programs, finance and closures

  • GCU Taking Steps to Open New College of Law, College of Construction and Industrial Technologies — PR Newswire
  • GCU moving forward with plans for new law school — Axios Phoenix
  • Anna Maria bankruptcy sale of property faces objection from neighbor — Higher Ed Dive
  • Saint Augustine's Wins Stay on Former Trustees' Legal Costs — Inside Higher Ed
  • Bankrupt Saint Augustine's Will Not Offer Fall Classes — Inside Higher Ed

Competitor Spotlight — ASU Online, Purdue Global, SNHU, UMGC

  • ASU reaches milestone enrollment — ASU News
  • UMGC expands degree offerings for 2026-27 academic year — GlobeNewswire
  • UMGC wins 2026 Tambellini Future Campus Award for AI-powered military credit initiative — GlobeNewswire

The Higher Ed News Digest is published every Monday and Thursday. The Competitor Spotlight tracks ASU Online, Purdue Global, SNHU and UMGC on a rolling two-week lookback.

One thing to watch: the significant part of the MIT report is not that AI can pass undergraduate written work — anyone teaching this year already knows that. It is the buried request that curriculum changes made in response to AI be allowed to bypass "fixed, multi-committee, year-long review processes." That is a governance recommendation, not a pedagogy one, and every faculty senate in the country is about to receive some version of it.

item.title: SPECIAL EDITION — The One Big Beautiful Bill Hits Campus
item.description:
Special edition. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act was signed on 4 July 2025, but almost everything in it that touches higher education took effect on 1 July 2026. This autumn is the first term run under the new rules. Fifteen reports, leading with what named institutions have actually done.

In this episode

  1. MIT closed two libraries — $200m of a $300m annual gap is the endowment tax alone
  2. Yale's tax bill is larger than its entire undergraduate financial aid budget
  3. Harvard cut doctoral admissions by more than three quarters in the sciences
  4. Notre Dame froze hiring and stopped starting new buildings
  5. The second tier: WashU, Stanford, Penn and Brown
  6. The plot twist — small wealthy colleges walked away untaxed
  7. Grad PLUS is gone, and two law schools have started lending their own money
  8. Which degrees count as "professional" is now in its fourth lawsuit
  9. The earnings test everyone fears has not yet touched anyone
  10. Workforce Pell is live, and the pipeline is far narrower than advertised
  11. RAP launches into a 576,000-application backlog
  12. The quieter hit: SNAP and Medicaid cost shifts are squeezing state budgets
  13. What WCET and WICHE are telling digital learning leaders
  14. The scoreboard: CBO, JCT and the ratings agencies
  15. One thing to watch — three dates that decide what this law actually did

One thing to watch: the visible damage and the consequential damage are in different places. The endowment tax produced everything photographable but raises $761m over ten years. The loan caps will reshape who goes to graduate school and will not show up in data until October at the earliest.

Sources

Endowment tax — institutional accounts

  • Major tax impact on MIT and its mission — MIT Office of the Provost
  • MIT to close multiple libraries in budget rebalancing — The Tech
  • Kornbluth on budgeting and financial aid — The Tech
  • University budget update, December 2025 — Yale Provost
  • Update on tax legislation — Yale President
  • Budget update FAQs — Yale Provost
  • Endowment tax FAQs — Harvard
  • FAS cuts PhD seats by more than half — The Harvard Crimson
  • Harvard's endowment and FY2025 deficit — Harvard Magazine
  • A message from the executive officers — University of Notre Dame
  • Federal legislation update — WashU Chancellor
  • Faculty Senate FY27 budget plan — Stanford
  • Penn's FY2027 budget, cost-cutting and layoffs — The Daily Pennsylvanian
  • Brown to face increased 4% endowment tax — The Brown Daily Herald
  • Endowment tax is leading to hiring freezes — PBS NewsHour
  • Wealthy universities cut PhDs and libraries — Christian Science Monitor

Loans, borrowing caps and the professional degree fight

  • Who borrows above the new limits — PEER Center, American University
  • St. Louis colleges respond to the new loan caps — First Alert 4
  • Santa Clara Law launches the PLEDGE scholarship — Santa Clara University
  • Unions sue Education Department over 'professional' degree rule — Higher Ed Dive
  • Social work, education still fighting for higher loan caps — Inside Higher Ed
  • ED clarifies how current students can access uncapped loans — Inside Higher Ed
  • Has the Graduate-School Collapse Begun? — The Chronicle of Higher Education
  • 46,000 borrowers move to the new repayment plan on day one — Forbes

Accountability, Workforce Pell and the state squeeze

  • STATS and Earnings Accountability final rule — Federal Register
  • How college programs measure up against the new standard — PEER Center
  • Almost half of colleges haven't fully submitted student data — Inside Higher Ed
  • Iowa college first to get ED's OK for Workforce Pell — Community College Daily
  • Workforce Pell is live. How's it going in the states? — Inside Higher Ed
  • States grapple with effects of OBBBA cuts on higher ed — Inside Higher Ed
  • SNAP cuts and state higher education budgets — TICAS

Digital learning and sector analysis

  • What the One Big Beautiful Bill Act means for digital learning — WCET Frontiers
  • One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025) — WICHE Policy Tracker
  • Budgetary effects of the student loan provisions — Congressional Budget Office
  • NASFAA and ACE on the first term under the new rules — NASFAA
  • Ratings agencies' 2026 higher ed outlooks — Higher Ed Dive

Verification notes: figures are institution-stated wherever possible. Deliberately excluded — the widely circulated $89m Dartmouth estimate, which models the rejected 14% House rate, and a single-source report that Princeton fell below the exemption threshold, which Princeton has not confirmed. Brown, Penn, Dartmouth and Vanderbilt have published no dollar figure for the 4% rate.
